# Amatriciana Bianca

## Ingredients

- 150 g guanciale, cut into strips
- 400 g spaghetti
- 1 small onion, optional, finely sliced
- 2 cloves of garlic, lightly crushed
- a glass of dry white wine
- 60 g pecorino romano, grated
- a pinch of chilli flakes
- salt and a little olive oil

## Steps

1. Render the guanciale in a dry pan over medium heat until the fat runs and the strips turn golden, then lift them out and set them aside.
2. If you want the onion, soften it now in the rendered fat until it is translucent, then add the crushed garlic and the chilli flakes for the last minute.
3. Pour in the glass of white wine and let it bubble down by half, scraping the base of the pan so nothing sticks.
4. Boil the spaghetti in well-salted water until al dente, saving a cup of the cooking water before you drain it.
5. Return the guanciale to the pan, add the drained pasta with a splash of the cooking water, and toss over low heat until the strands are coated.
6. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the pecorino romano until it melts into a loose, glossy sauce.

## Notes

This is the white version, so there is no tomato in it at all. The colour comes from the wine, the rendered fat and the cheese, and that is the whole point of the dish. I use a dry unoaked white because anything sweet or heavily oaked fights the guanciale. The onion is genuinely optional; some cooks in Amatrice would not dream of it, and I only add it when the guanciale is lean and needs a little sweetness to round it out. The wine should reduce until the sharp alcohol smell is gone, otherwise the sauce tastes raw. Pecorino romano is the cheese to use, and parmesan makes the dish flatter and less salty. Watch the heat at the end, because cheese added to a screaming pan will seize into strings. If the sauce breaks, a spoonful of warm cooking water and a hard toss usually pulls it back together. The spaghetti needs to be firm so the strands stay separate in the pan. Serve at once in warm bowls, with the same wine you cooked with, and nothing else on the plate but a piece of bread to mop up. I have made this with bacon in a pinch and it works, but the smoky cure of proper guanciale is what carries the dish, and the wine reduction needs that fat to balance against.
